title: Mass of a body by the principle of moments
objective: To determine the mass of a given body using a metre scale and the principle of moments.
To verify that at balance the anticlockwise moment equals the clockwise moment.
To show why the metre scale must first be balanced at its centre of gravity.

theory.statement: A rigid body is in rotational equilibrium when the total anticlockwise moment about any point equals the total clockwise moment about that point. A metre scale balanced on a knife edge is such a body: hanging an unknown mass on one side and a known mass on the other, and adjusting until the scale is level, makes the two moments equal.
theory.derivationNote: The moment of a force about a pivot is the product of the force and the perpendicular distance from the pivot to its line of action. If an unknown mass m hangs at a distance d₁ on one side and a known mass M at d₂ on the other, then at balance m·g·d₁ = M·g·d₂. The g cancels, leaving m·d₁ = M·d₂ and hence m = M·d₂/d₁. The metre scale has weight of its own, acting at its centre of gravity. If the knife edge is placed exactly at that centre of gravity, the weight of the scale acts through the pivot and its moment is zero, which is why the bare scale must be balanced first. If the pivot were anywhere else, the moment of the scale itself would have to be included and the simple formula would no longer hold. Note also that this measures MASS without ever using the value of g, exactly as a beam balance does.
keyEquations: Moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot
At balance: anticlockwise moment = clockwise moment
The weight of the scale has zero moment when the pivot is at its centre of gravity

apparatus.name: Metre scale
apparatus.spec: uniform, wooden, with a hole or groove for the knife edge
apparatus.why: The rigid body whose equilibrium is studied; also the ruler for the distances

apparatus.name: Knife edge on a stand
apparatus.why: Provides a well defined pivot with negligible friction

apparatus.name: Known masses
apparatus.spec: 20 g, 50 g and 100 g from a weight box
apparatus.why: Provide the known moment against which the unknown is compared

apparatus.name: Unknown body
apparatus.spec: with a hook or a loop of thread
apparatus.why: The body whose mass is to be found

apparatus.name: Thread loops
apparatus.why: Hang the masses; light loops add negligible moment of their own

procedure.text: Balance the bare metre scale on the knife edge and note the mark at which it balances. This is its centre of gravity.
Keep the knife edge at that mark for the whole experiment, so the weight of the scale exerts no moment.
Suspend the unknown body from a thread loop on one side of the knife edge and note its position.
Suspend a known mass on the other side and slide it until the scale is horizontal again.
When the scale is level, note the positions of both masses and calculate their distances from the knife edge.
Repeat with the unknown at a different distance, and again with a different known mass.
Calculate m = M·d₂/d₁ for each set of readings and take the mean.

steps: d₁ = distance of the unknown mass from the knife edge
d₂ = distance of the known mass from the knife edge
Take the mean of m over all the trials

expectedResult.statement: Body P has a mass of about 74.5 g. The same value is obtained with different known masses and at different distances, which is what confirms the principle of moments rather than merely applying it once.

safety: Clamp the knife-edge stand firmly so that it cannot topple when the masses are hung.
Keep fingers clear beneath the hanging masses.
Support the metre scale while loading it; a scale that slips off the knife edge can break.
Handle the knife edge carefully — it is genuinely sharp.
sourcesOfError: The knife edge not being exactly at the centre of gravity of the scale.
The metre scale bending slightly under heavy loads, so the distances are not truly horizontal.
Thread loops of unequal weight, or loops that slip along the scale.
Judging by eye when the scale is exactly horizontal.
Parallax when reading the positions against the scale markings.
Friction at the knife edge, which lets the scale rest slightly off balance.

viva.question: State the principle of moments.
viva.expectedConcept: When a body is in rotational equilibrium, the sum of the anticlockwise moments about any point equals the sum of the clockwise moments about that point.
viva.commonMisconception: Stating it as forces balancing rather than moments.

viva.question: Define the moment of a force.
viva.expectedConcept: It is the product of the force and the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force. Its SI unit is the newton metre.
viva.commonMisconception: Using the distance to the point of application rather than the perpendicular distance.

viva.question: Why must the metre scale be balanced at its centre of gravity first?
viva.expectedConcept: The scale has weight of its own, acting at its centre of gravity. If the knife edge is placed there, that weight acts through the pivot and its moment about the pivot is zero. Anywhere else it contributes an extra moment which would have to be included in the calculation.
viva.answerLogic: A force through the pivot has no moment.
viva.commonMisconception: Thinking the scale is weightless or that its weight always cancels.

viva.question: Does the value of g affect your result?
viva.expectedConcept: No. The weights on both sides are proportional to g, so it cancels from m·g·d₁ = M·g·d₂. The method compares masses, not weights, and would give the same answer on the Moon.
viva.commonMisconception: Assuming any experiment involving weight must depend on g.

viva.question: What is the centre of gravity of a body?
viva.expectedConcept: The point at which the whole weight of the body may be taken to act. For a uniform metre scale it lies at the geometrical centre, near the 50 cm mark.
viva.commonMisconception: Confusing it with the centre of the pivot.

viva.question: The unknown mass is moved further from the knife edge. What happens to the balancing position?
viva.expectedConcept: Its moment increases in proportion to the distance, so the known mass must also move further out to restore balance. The ratio d₂/d₁ stays the same, which is why the calculated mass is unchanged.
viva.commonMisconception: Expecting a different value of m at a different distance.

viva.question: Why is it better to repeat the experiment with a different known mass rather than simply repeating it?
viva.expectedConcept: Repeating with the same mass at the same place tests only the repeatability of the reading. Using a different known mass gives an independent determination, so agreement between them is genuine evidence that the principle holds.
viva.commonMisconception: Treating any three readings as three independent results.

viva.question: What happens if the unknown mass is hung exactly at the knife edge?
viva.expectedConcept: Its line of action passes through the pivot, so its moment about the pivot is zero whatever its size. It cannot be balanced against anything and no measurement is possible.
viva.answerLogic: Zero perpendicular distance means zero moment.
viva.commonMisconception: Thinking a heavy mass must always produce a turning effect.

viva.question: Give two everyday applications of the principle of moments.
viva.expectedConcept: A see-saw, where a lighter child sits further from the pivot to balance a heavier one; a common beam balance; a crowbar or spanner, where a long handle gives a large moment for a small force; and the counterweight on a crane.
viva.commonMisconception: Describing them as examples of energy conservation instead.

viva.question: Would this method work if the metre scale were not uniform?
viva.expectedConcept: Yes, provided the knife edge is placed at the point where the bare scale balances, which is its centre of gravity wherever that happens to be. That point need not be the 50 cm mark. What matters is that the weight of the scale acts through the pivot.
viva.answerLogic: Balance the bare scale, wherever its CG lies.
viva.commonMisconception: Assuming the centre of gravity is always at the geometrical centre.

preLab.question: A body is in rotational equilibrium when:
options: It is at the centre of gravity

preLab.question: The knife edge is placed at the centre of gravity of the scale so that:
options: The weight of the scale exerts no moment

duringLab.question: Record at least three balanced readings.
Use more than one known mass, so the check is independent.

postLab.question: State the mass of body P in gram.
You moved the knife edge to the 45 cm mark and kept the same formula. Your result would be:
options: Wrong, because the weight of the scale now has a moment
postLab.feedback: Off the centre of gravity, the weight of the scale exerts its own moment which the simple formula ignores.

postLab.question: The value of g does not appear in the final formula because:
options: It cancels from both sides of the moment equation
postLab.feedback: m·g·d₁ = M·g·d₂, so g cancels and the method compares masses directly.
